awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: RAPID: Collecting, archiving, and characterizing residual ash, transported ash, and particulate matter from the Los Angeles fire
awd_abstract_narration:
The wildfires in Los Angeles in January 2025 were the most destructive disaster in recent California history. While much is known about wildfire smoke, a significant knowledge gap remains about how far toxic chemicals spread from the active burn areas. To find out, Dr. Spada and his community partners set up an air monitoring network at locations across the Los Angeles area, downwind of the largest fires. These monitors continuously collected smoke, dust, and ash while the fires were still active and throughout cleanup activities. For millions of Los Angeles residents, these measurements will provide answers about how much toxic chemicals were released, how far they traveled, and when is safe to return to burned areas. Insights gained from this project will help bridge our knowledge gaps and allow us to be better prepared for the future.

This RAPID grant will support field research to collect, archive, and characterize samples during and immediately after the Los Angeles (LA) fires that started on January 7th, 2025. The aim of the project is to quantify the concentration and determine the speciation of toxic elements in airborne particulate matter (PM) collected during and following the fires. Specific objectives are: 1) To collect and archive PM during and following the fires; 2) To quantify the concentrations of elements in all samples; 3) To disseminate validated findings appropriately in order for public health and government agencies to provide accurate recommendations for residents returning to their homes; and 4) To share collected materials with scientific collaborators to maximize the learning potential from this unique scenario. Ambient PM was collected using cascading impactors with rotating stages at four locations distributed across the LA area. Samples will be analyzed initially at Crocker Nuclear Lab’s 76-inch isochronous cyclotron using Proton-Induced X-ray Emission (PIXE), Proton Elastic Scattering Analysis (PESA), and Rutherford Backscattering Analysis (RBA). These combined measurements provide quantitative results for non-volatile H, C, and O alongside Na – Br and Pb. To the team's knowledge, this will be the first dataset of its kind. Subsequent measurements will include Synchrotron-induced X-ray Fluorescence (SXRF) at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource to measure higher atomic weight elements such as cadmium, cesium, and rare earth elements. Supporting measurements will include mass concentrations via soft-beta ray attenuation and broadband optical spectroscopy, which will enable factorization and source apportionment analyses by future collaborators. The sampling campaign captures PM during the fire, immediately after the fires were put out, while the burn areas were still smoldering, and during cleanup activities that may resuspend toxic substances. These results will provide information on the exposures to first and second responders and to residents downwind of the fire areas.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Overview of the Collaborative Research: RAPID: Collecting, archiving, and characterizing residual ash, transported ash, and particulate matter from the Los Angeles fire

Award #2521485

 

Community Volunteers Lead the Way

This rapid response study relied heavily on the Parents Against Santa Susana Field Lab (PASSFL) community group.

  • Founders Melissa Bumstead and Jeni Knack were critical to the project, finding over 20 volunteer homes to host monitoring equipment within just 48 hours.
  • Going above and beyond hosting, Bumstead and Knack personally collected ash samples and wore personal air monitors in the burn areas.
  • To ensure their safety while gathering data, they wore full personal protective equipment.
  • PASSFL also drafted community-accessible safety procedures to help others properly use protective gear when going into burn areas.

How We Measured the Smoke

To understand exactly what was in the air, the research team used highly specialized equipment and analytical techniques.

  • The team deployed cascading air samplers at four locations: Pasadena, Santa Monica, Hollywood, and West Hills.
  • These devices continuously gathered particulate matter, ultimately collecting over 10,000 individual samples.
  • Project funding allowed the laboratory to analyze approximately 25 % of these samples, resulting in about 2,900 measurements of elementals, such as metals and non-metals.
  • To identify specific chemicals, the lab used a technique called ion beam analysis. This uses a proton beam to quantify 26 different chemical parameters.
  • For the personal monitors worn by the volunteers, the team used two different methods to cross-check accuracy: energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence (ED-XRF) and inductively coupled plasma – time of flight – mass spectrometry (ICP-TOF-MS).
  • Using multiple techniques is highly effective because ED-XRF and ion beam analysis are better at detecting lighter elements like sodium and sulfur, while mass spectrometry is better for identifying heavier elements.

Comparing the Four Neighborhoods

Because the monitors were spread across the greater Los Angeles metropolitan area, researchers were able to track how the smoke changed as it traveled away from the Eaton and Palisades fires. The distance from the fires directly affected the types and sizes of particles in the air:

  • Pasadena and Santa Monica (Closest to the Fires): Because these areas were right next to the active burn zones, they experienced the most direct impacts. The air here contained the highest concentrations of "coarse" particles, including large spikes in silicon and raw ash. These larger, heavier particles tend to fall out of the air quickly before they can travel far.
  • Hollywood (Intermediate Distance): As the smoke moved toward Hollywood, the particle profile shifted. The heavy, coarse ash dropped off, but monitors picked up a steady, high presence of fine and submicron smoke particles. These smaller particles are light enough to stay suspended in the air longer and travel further on wind currents.
  • West Hills (North of the Palisades and Eaton Fires): Located furthest from the largest fire areas, West Hills generally recorded the lowest overall particulate concentrations of the four sites. However, the monitors still detected elevated levels of very-fine particles and specific combustion chemicals, demonstrating how far the fire's chemical footprint extended across the region.

A Breakdown of Particle Sizes

Analyzing the specific sizes of the particles helps researchers trace their origins:

  • Larger Particles (Above 1 µm): Generally coming from natural grinding and abrasion, elements like iron, titanium, calcium, potassium, and silicon were detected in 100% of the samples in this size range. These elements are often associated with soil dust.
  • Smaller Submicron Particles (Below 1 µm): These tiny particles are typically produced by active combustion and burning.
  • Silicon Levels: Silicon stood out across all size categories, but was particularly concentrated in the coarse (10 to 2.5 µm) and very-fine (0.26 to 0.09 µm) ranges in Pasadena and Santa Monica. The coarse silicon is likely from soil dust but the very-fine silicon source is still unknown.
  • Sulfur Peaking: Sulfur concentrations were highest in the mid-to-small range (0.56 to 0.26 µm), which is likely in the form of sulfate. Other major sources of submicron sulfur include diesel emissions and fuel burning.
  • Titanium Anomaly: Researchers noted an unusually high detection rate for very-fine titanium particles, which they suspect may be related to burned paint.

 

Key Chemical Discoveries

  • Reassuringly, the study observed relatively low overall detection rates for toxic elements like arsenic and lead across the neighborhood monitors.
  • However, when comparing the air samples to standard burned vegetation, researchers found a measurable enrichment (higher than expected natural levels) of several human-made metals, including copper, zinc, tin, antimony, and lead.
  • There was also a notable enrichment of indium. Since indium is used to create transparent conductive coatings for touchscreens in electronics, this could have contributed to the smoke plume.

Takeaway

This project produced a unique dataset of size-resolved chemistry that will help public health researchers understand the toxicity of urban wildfire smoke. Residents and first responders will have better information for future wildfires.
